item.title: 🚨 Microsoft Purview Roadmap 549288: Making SharePoint DLP Smarter with Adaptive Scopes
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft Purview continues to evolve from a collection of individual compliance controls into a much more dynamic governance platform. One particularly useful development is Roadmap ID 549288: Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention – Adaptive Scopes for DLP for SharePoint. And while the headline might sound like another technical DLP feature, the real benefit is much […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Purview continues to evolve from a collection of individual compliance controls into a much more dynamic governance platform. One particularly useful development is Roadmap ID 549288: Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention – Adaptive Scopes for DLP for SharePoint.

And while the headline might sound like another technical DLP feature, the real benefit is much more interesting:

Your DLP policies can become more responsive to how your SharePoint environment actually changes.

Microsoft describes Adaptive Scopes for SharePoint as a dynamic capability that allows administrators to target DLP policies based on attributes such as site URL, site name or custom site metadata, rather than relying solely on manually maintained lists of sites.

That has potentially significant implications for organisations trying to scale Microsoft Purview governance.

The problem with static DLP

Let’s imagine your organisation has 500 SharePoint sites.

You have a DLP policy designed to protect sensitive information on a particular group of sites – perhaps sites belonging to a particular business function, containing a particular type of information, or matching particular organisational criteria.

With a traditional static approach, administrators have to maintain the scope of those sites.

And that’s where things become difficult.

SharePoint environments don’t stand still.

New sites are created.

Existing sites change.

Business units reorganise.

Projects start and finish.

Site properties change.

The result?

Your DLP policy can potentially become disconnected from the environment it was designed to protect.

You might have a perfectly designed policy — but an outdated scope.

And that’s a governance problem.

Enter Adaptive Scopes

This is where Roadmap 549288 becomes interesting.

Instead of thinking:

“Which sites do I need to put into this DLP policy?”

you can start thinking:

“Which sites meet the criteria that this DLP policy should apply to?”

That’s a significant change in mindset.

Adaptive Scopes can automatically evaluate SharePoint site attributes and dynamically determine which sites should be included or excluded from the policy. Microsoft specifically describes this as continuously evaluating site properties and automatically adjusting scope as the environment changes.

So rather than constantly maintaining a list of locations, you define the governance logic.

The environment can then help maintain the scope.

Benefit 1: Less administration

Probably the most obvious benefit is reduced administrative overhead.

Consider an organisation with hundreds or thousands of SharePoint sites.

Maintaining static site lists can become a significant operational task.

Every time a site is created or changed, somebody potentially needs to consider:

Does this site need to be added to the DLP policy?

Adaptive Scopes can reduce that manual maintenance by allowing policy targeting to be based on attributes.

Microsoft highlights this reduction in manual list maintenance as one of the key benefits of the capability.

That means administrators can spend less time maintaining policy membership and more time thinking about whether the policy itself is appropriate.

Benefit 2: Governance that keeps up with the business

This is, in my opinion, one of the biggest benefits.

Traditional governance often struggles because the organisation changes faster than the governance model.

A new SharePoint site appears.

The governance team doesn’t know about it.

The site contains sensitive information.

The DLP policy doesn’t cover it.

That’s not necessarily a failure of the DLP technology.

It’s a failure of static governance in a dynamic environment.

Adaptive Scopes provide an opportunity to make the policy more responsive.

If a newly created site meets the defined criteria, it can automatically fall within the appropriate scope. Microsoft specifically states that this helps ensure new or updated sites are protected without requiring manual list maintenance.

That’s a much more scalable governance model.

Benefit 3: Better scalability

This becomes increasingly important as organisations expand their use of SharePoint.

You might start with:

50 sites

and manually manage them relatively easily.

Then you reach:

500 sites.

Then:

5,000 sites.

At some point, manually maintaining policy scopes becomes increasingly difficult.

Microsoft’s documentation notes that Adaptive Scopes can eliminate the 100-site static policy limit, while providing more granular and automated targeting.

That makes this particularly relevant for large organisations and organisations experiencing rapid SharePoint growth.

Benefit 4: More precise policy targeting

More sites covered doesn’t necessarily mean better governance.

The goal isn’t:

“Put every site into every DLP policy.”

That’s likely to create unnecessary policy complexity and potentially overwhelm users with controls and notifications.

The real goal is:

Apply the right policy to the right information in the right locations.

Adaptive Scopes provide more granular targeting based on site characteristics.

That allows organisations to think more carefully about their policy architecture.

For example, you might have different governance requirements for:

  • Finance sites
  • HR sites
  • Legal sites
  • Research sites
  • Customer information
  • Highly confidential projects

Instead of relying purely on manually maintained site lists, you can use attributes to help determine where the relevant DLP controls should apply.

Benefit 5: Better protection against governance drift

This is perhaps the benefit that doesn’t immediately jump out from Microsoft’s technical description.

I’d call it governance drift.

Governance drift happens when your policies were correct when they were created – but the environment has changed.

Your DLP policy says:

“Protect these 75 sites.”

Six months later:

  • 20 new sites exist.
  • 10 sites have changed purpose.
  • 5 have been retired.
  • 15 new projects have been created.

The policy might still technically be working.

But its scope may no longer reflect the organisation.

Adaptive Scopes can help reduce that gap by dynamically evaluating site characteristics.

That’s important because governance isn’t simply about creating policies.

It’s about ensuring those policies remain relevant.

And this matters even more in the age of Copilot

There’s a bigger story here.

Microsoft 365 Copilot can work with information that users already have permission to access.

That makes SharePoint governance increasingly important in an AI-enabled organisation.

If your SharePoint environment contains:

  • overshared information
  • poorly governed sites
  • sensitive information
  • outdated permissions
  • inappropriate content

Then AI can make the consequences of poor governance more visible.

This is why improvements to Purview DLP shouldn’t be viewed simply as another compliance feature.

They’re part of a much bigger shift towards:

AI-ready information governance.

As one Microsoft-focused analysis of this roadmap points out, the real leadership question is increasingly about whether organisations have the governance discipline to let AI operate safely and at scale.

The bigger lesson: stop governing lists, start governing conditions

This is the part I find most interesting about Roadmap 549288.

Traditional governance often looks like this:

“Here is a list of things we currently know about.”

Modern governance increasingly needs to look like:

“Here are the conditions under which this policy should apply.”

That’s a subtle but very important change.

Instead of constantly asking:

“Did we remember to add that site?”

you can start asking:

“Does that site meet the conditions that require this protection?”

That’s a much more sustainable approach.

What does this mean for organisations?

If you’re responsible for Microsoft Purview, DLP or SharePoint governance, this is a good opportunity to revisit your existing approach.

Ask yourself:

1. How much of our DLP scoping is manually maintained?

If the answer is “a lot”, there may be an opportunity to simplify.

2. How quickly does our governance respond to new SharePoint sites?

If it relies on somebody remembering to update a policy, there’s a potential gap.

3. Are we using site attributes effectively?

Think about whether your existing SharePoint metadata and structure could support more intelligent governance.

4. Are our DLP policies aligned with business requirements?

Don’t use Adaptive Scopes simply because they’re available.

First understand what you’re trying to protect and why.

5. Is our SharePoint governance ready for AI?

This is increasingly important as Copilot and other AI capabilities make organisational information more accessible and actionable.

When is it arriving?

Microsoft originally announced Adaptive Scopes for SharePoint for 2026. The roadmap currently identifies Roadmap ID 549288 as a Microsoft Purview capability for the worldwide standard multi-tenant environment.

The timeline has changed during development, so organisations should treat Microsoft’s roadmap dates as estimates rather than fixed commitments. Microsoft itself notes that roadmap release dates are subject to change.

The associated Message Center announcement currently indicates General Availability beginning in late August 2026 and completing by late September 2026.

item.title: 🚨 What if we stopped retaining files simply because nobody has deleted them?
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft Purview is bringing “last accessed” retention to SharePoint and OneDrive One of the biggest challenges in Microsoft 365 isn’t necessarily creating information. It’s getting rid of information we no longer need. Over the years, organisations accumulate enormous amounts of content in SharePoint and OneDrive: And often, nobody knows whether any of it is still […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Purview is bringing “last accessed” retention to SharePoint and OneDrive

One of the biggest challenges in Microsoft 365 isn’t necessarily creating information.

It’s getting rid of information we no longer need.

Over the years, organisations accumulate enormous amounts of content in SharePoint and OneDrive:

  • Old project documents
  • Historical reports
  • Superseded policies
  • Previous versions of presentations
  • Outdated spreadsheets
  • Former project team information
  • Documents that haven’t been opened for years

And often, nobody knows whether any of it is still relevant.

Microsoft Purview Roadmap ID 472030 introduces an interesting new approach: the ability to apply retention to SharePoint and OneDrive files based on when they were last accessed.

The latest Microsoft Message Center update says Preview is expected to begin in late October 2026, with General Availability beginning in late December 2026 and completing by late January 2027.

And I think this could be much more significant than it initially appears.

We’ve traditionally thought about retention differently

Historically, retention tends to revolve around questions such as:

When was this document created?

When was it modified?

When was it labelled?

How long do we need to retain it?

Those are important questions.

But there’s another question that can tell us something very useful:

When did anyone last actually use it?

That changes the conversation.

A document created five years ago isn’t necessarily obsolete.

A document modified five years ago isn’t necessarily obsolete either.

But if nobody in the organisation has accessed it for five years, that’s potentially a very different story.

Introducing “last accessed”

With this capability, administrators will be able to use when items were last accessed as a retention control when configuring retention policies and labels for supported SharePoint and OneDrive content.

For example, an organisation might decide that certain content should be reviewed or removed when it hasn’t been accessed for a specified period.

This gives information governance teams another dimension to consider:

Not just how old is the information?

But:

How recently has the information actually been used?

Imagine this scenario

You have a SharePoint site containing 250,000 documents.

Some were created last month.

Some were created ten years ago.

Some are actively used every day.

Others haven’t been opened since 2018.

Today, your retention strategy might struggle to distinguish between them if it’s primarily based on age or other metadata.

With a last-accessed approach, you can start to identify a very different category:

Information that has effectively become dormant.

That doesn’t automatically mean:

“Delete it.”

And this is an important distinction.

It means:

“This information hasn’t been accessed for X period — perhaps it should now be subject to a different retention decision.”

That’s much more interesting.

This could be a major information governance improvement

One of the biggest problems with retention is that organisations often retain information just in case.

Nobody wants to be responsible for deleting something that might eventually be needed.

So the safest decision becomes:

“Keep it.”

Then another year passes.

Then another.

Eventually, the organisation has millions of documents that nobody knows whether they still need.

This creates data hoarding.

And data hoarding creates problems.

More data means:

  • More information to govern
  • More information to classify
  • More information to search
  • More information to protect
  • More information potentially accessible to users
  • More information potentially available to AI

Which brings us to perhaps the most interesting part of this update.

The Copilot connection

Microsoft explicitly says this capability can help improve the quality and relevance of Microsoft 365 Copilot responses by helping organisations remove obsolete data.

Think about that.

The problem isn’t simply:

“We have too many files.”

It’s:

“We have too much old information that may still be available when people – and AI – are looking for answers.”

If your organisation has years of obsolete documents sitting in SharePoint, they can potentially become part of the information landscape that users and AI interact with.

Good AI governance therefore starts with something much more fundamental:

Good information governance.

You can’t expect AI to produce consistently useful answers if your underlying information estate is full of outdated material.

But be careful: old doesn’t mean useless

This is where governance teams need to exercise caution.

Completely obsolete.

Or it could be:

Extremely important.

Consider:

  • A legal agreement
  • A historical financial record
  • A regulatory record
  • A corporate governance document
  • A long-term research record
  • Evidence required for litigation
  • A document subject to a legal hold

Nobody accessing the document doesn’t necessarily mean the organisation is allowed to delete it.

This is why last accessed should be treated as a governance signal, not an automatic deletion decision.

Retention requirements, legal holds, regulatory obligations and business requirements still matter.

The real opportunity: information lifecycle management

For me, this is where Roadmap 472030 becomes particularly interesting.

It potentially allows organisations to think about information as having a lifecycle:

Active

People are regularly accessing and using the information.

↓

Dormant

The information hasn’t been accessed for a significant period.

↓

Review

The organisation determines whether it still has business, legal or regulatory value.

↓

Retain or dispose

The information is either retained appropriately or disposed of according to policy.

That’s a much more intelligent information lifecycle.

It could also expose some uncomfortable truths

Imagine running this across your organisation and discovering:

40% of the documents in a particular SharePoint estate haven’t been accessed in five years.

That’s an interesting finding.

You might discover:

  • Old project sites
  • Abandoned collaboration spaces
  • Duplicate content
  • Historical information
  • Orphaned documents
  • Data that should have been deleted years ago

And that creates an opportunity.

Rather than simply buying more storage and accepting the ever-growing data estate, you can start asking:

Why are we keeping this?

That’s a much healthier information governance question.

What should organisations start thinking about?

Even though Microsoft says no action is required before rollout, this is a good opportunity to review your current information lifecycle strategy.

I’d start by asking:

1. Do we know how much dormant content we have?

Not just how much data exists.

How much hasn’t been accessed?

2. Do we have retention policies that reflect business value?

Are we retaining information simply because we’re afraid to delete it?

3. Are our SharePoint sites being actively governed?

Do abandoned sites have an owner?

4. Could obsolete information be affecting Copilot?

Could old documents be making it harder for users – or AI – to find the information that actually matters?

5. What information must never be automatically disposed of?

Legal, regulatory and business-critical information needs appropriate safeguards.

The Jim Talks takeaway

For me, the real significance of this update isn’t the new retention setting.

It’s the question it encourages us to ask:

“Is this information still useful?”

We’ve become very good at creating and storing information.

We’re becoming much better at protecting it.

But many organisations are still struggling with the third part:

Knowing when to let it go.

And as Microsoft 365 becomes increasingly AI-driven, this becomes even more important.

Because the future isn’t simply about having more information.

It’s about having the right information.

Information that is current.

Information that is trustworthy.

Information that is appropriately protected.

And information that is actually worth keeping.

Roadmap ID 472030 could be a small Purview feature with a surprisingly big information governance impact.

item.title: 🚨 Microsoft Purview is coming for the data you’ve already forgotten about
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Your biggest data protection problem might already be sitting in SharePoint When organisations talk about information protection, the conversation often focuses on what happens from now on. New documents get created. New files are uploaded. Users apply sensitivity labels. Policies are configured. DLP is enabled. Everything looks nicely governed. But there is a problem. ❓ […]
item.content:encoded:
Your biggest data protection problem might already be sitting in SharePoint

When organisations talk about information protection, the conversation often focuses on what happens from now on.

New documents get created.

New files are uploaded.

Users apply sensitivity labels.

Policies are configured.

DLP is enabled.

Everything looks nicely governed.

But there is a problem.

What about the millions of files that were created before all of those controls existed?

That’s where Microsoft Purview Roadmap ID 499076 gets interesting.

Microsoft is introducing a capability that will allow administrators to scan existing files at rest in SharePoint and OneDrive for Business for sensitive information. The roadmap currently lists the feature as In development, with General Availability targeted for December 2026.

And this could be a very useful addition to the Purview toolkit.

The forgotten data problem

Think about a typical Microsoft 365 environment.

An organisation may have been using SharePoint and OneDrive for years.

During that time, users have created:

  • Contracts
  • HR documents
  • Financial spreadsheets
  • Customer information
  • Employee records
  • Project documentation
  • Commercial plans
  • Legal documents
  • Reports
  • Presentations
  • Old archives

Some of these files may be labelled.

Some may be protected by DLP.

Some may have been automatically classified.

And some may have never been evaluated for sensitive information at all.

This creates what I would call the “legacy data problem.”

Your organisation may have excellent information protection controls today…

…but that doesn’t necessarily mean your historical data has been through those controls.

Why “at rest” is important

The wording in Microsoft’s roadmap is particularly interesting:

“existing files at rest”

This is important because Microsoft already has mechanisms that evaluate content when it is created, edited or otherwise processed.

Microsoft’s current guidance explains that files in SharePoint and OneDrive can remain unclassified if they haven’t been edited or touched, and that on-demand scanning can be used to evaluate historical content.

That’s a huge distinction.

Imagine a document created in 2019.

It hasn’t been opened since.

Nobody has edited it.

It contains sensitive information.

Your organisation introduced a much better Purview classification strategy in 2025.

Does that automatically mean the 2019 document has been evaluated against your new classification approach?

Not necessarily.

That’s the gap this type of capability is designed to address.

This could change how organisations approach data discovery

One of the biggest challenges with information governance is knowing what you actually have.

Organisations often have policies saying:

“Sensitive information must be protected.”

But the more difficult question is:

“Where is the sensitive information?”

And that’s much harder to answer when you’re dealing with millions of files.

This new capability moves the conversation from:

“We have policies.” to: “We’ve actually evaluated our existing data.”

That’s a significant difference.

Imagine what you could discover

An organisation could potentially uncover things like:

Old HR information

A spreadsheet containing employee information from several years ago.

Financial information

Historical financial reports containing sensitive commercial data.

Customer information

Legacy customer datasets sitting in an old SharePoint site.

Contracts

Commercial agreements containing confidential terms.

Credentials and secrets

Sensitive authentication-related information accidentally stored in documents.

The important point isn’t simply finding the files, it’s understanding where your protection gaps actually exist.

This isn’t just a scanning exercise

I’d argue that organisations shouldn’t approach this feature as:

“Let’s scan everything and see what happens.”

That’s potentially a recipe for an enormous amount of data.

Instead, this should become part of a structured information governance exercise.

Think about the process as:

Discover → Classify → Assess → Protect → Remediate → Monitor

Discover

Find sensitive information that already exists.

Classify

Understand what type of sensitive information you’ve found.

Assess

Determine whether the information is appropriately protected.

Protect

Apply appropriate sensitivity labels, DLP controls or other safeguards.

Remediate

Move, restrict, delete or otherwise address information that shouldn’t exist where it currently does.

Monitor

Continue looking for new gaps.

That’s a much more mature approach than simply running a scan.

The relationship with sensitivity labels

This is where things become particularly interesting for Purview administrators.

Finding sensitive information doesn’t automatically mean that the file has an appropriate sensitivity label.

Microsoft’s current Purview guidance highlights the importance of automatically applying sensitivity labels to existing SharePoint and OneDrive content and notes that service-side auto-labelling can apply to existing files.

So imagine discovering:

10,000 files containing sensitive information

The next question becomes:

How many of those files are actually protected?

And then:

How many should be labelled?

And:

Are the labels appropriate?

This is where scanning becomes the beginning of the governance process rather than the end.

Don’t confuse discovery with protection

This is an important point.

Finding sensitive information isn’t the same as protecting it.

You could scan your entire SharePoint estate and discover thousands of sensitive documents.

But if you don’t have an appropriate response strategy, you’ve simply created a very large report.

The real value comes from connecting discovery to action.

For example:

Sensitive information detected

↓

No sensitivity label

↓

Assess business context

↓

Apply appropriate label

↓

Apply DLP controls

↓

Monitor

That’s where Purview becomes much more powerful.

There’s also an AI governance angle

And this is perhaps where I think this update becomes particularly relevant.

We’re entering an era where AI tools such as Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents can make it easier to discover and work with organisational information.

That makes the quality of your underlying data governance increasingly important.

If your SharePoint environment contains years of poorly classified, overshared or sensitive content, simply deploying Copilot doesn’t make that problem disappear.

In fact, AI can make existing governance weaknesses more important.

The better question isn’t:

“Have we deployed Copilot?” It’s “Is the data that Copilot can potentially work with appropriately governed?”

That’s why data discovery and information protection are becoming fundamental parts of AI governance.

What should organisations start thinking about?

Although Microsoft currently lists this as In development, with GA targeted for December 2026, I’d start thinking about the implications now.

Ask yourself:

1. How much historical data do we have?

Do you know how many files exist across SharePoint and OneDrive?

2. How much of that data has actually been classified?

Not how much could be classified.

How much has actually been evaluated?

3. Where are your high-risk locations?

Which SharePoint sites contain the most sensitive information?

4. What happens when sensitive information is discovered?

Do you have a defined remediation process?

5. Are your labels appropriate?

Finding a sensitive document is only useful if you can determine what protection it actually requires.

6. Are you ready for AI?

If Copilot and agents are increasingly working with organisational information, your information protection strategy becomes even more important.

The Jim Talks takeaway

For me, the most interesting thing about Roadmap 499076 isn’t the scanning capability itself.

It’s the principle behind it.

You can’t govern data you haven’t discovered.

And organisations have accumulated an enormous amount of data over the years.

Some of it is valuable.

Some of it is obsolete.

Some of it is sensitive.

Some of it is duplicated.

And some of it probably shouldn’t be there anymore.

The next phase of Microsoft Purview isn’t just about protecting new data.

It’s about finally shining a light on the data that’s been sitting quietly in the background for years.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all is:

“What would we discover if we scanned everything we’ve been ignoring?”

That could be where the really interesting findings begin.

Microsoft Purview Roadmap ID: 499076
Status: In development
Target GA: December 2026

item.title: 🚨 Microsoft Purview gets another layer of protection for Copilot web searches
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: What happens when Copilot needs to search the web? Microsoft 365 Copilot has become an increasingly powerful way for users to find information, summarise content and get answers without having to manually search across multiple sources. But there is an important question for organisations:  What happens when the information being used by Copilot contains sensitive […]
item.content:encoded:
What happens when Copilot needs to search the web?

Microsoft 365 Copilot has become an increasingly powerful way for users to find information, summarise content and get answers without having to manually search across multiple sources.

But there is an important question for organisations:

 What happens when the information being used by Copilot contains sensitive data?

Microsoft is now expanding Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to address exactly this scenario.

The new capability, identified on the Microsoft 365 Roadmap as RM565870, is designed to help prevent Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Chat from using sensitive information in external web searches.

And for organisations thinking seriously about AI governance, this is an important development.

 The problem: Copilot meets the public web

One of the attractions of Copilot is its ability to combine organisational information with information from the wider web.

That creates an interesting governance challenge.

Imagine a user is working with sensitive organisational information and asks Copilot a question that requires an external web search.

Without appropriate controls, organisations have to consider whether sensitive information could potentially become part of that external search interaction.

This is where the new Purview capability comes in.

Microsoft describes the feature as a real-time control designed to mitigate data leakage and oversharing risks by preventing Copilot from using sensitive data for external web searches.

In simple terms:

If the information is considered sensitive, Purview can prevent Copilot from using it when carrying out an external web search.

 Why this matters for AI governance

This is an important distinction.

AI governance isn’t simply about deciding:

“Can our employees use Copilot?”

The more important questions are becoming:

  • What information can Copilot access?
  • What information can Copilot use?
  • Where can that information go?
  • What happens when Copilot interacts with external services?
  • What controls prevent sensitive information from leaving the organisational boundary?

This latest DLP capability is another example of Microsoft moving towards more granular control over how AI interacts with organisational data.

It’s about controlling the data, not stopping the AI

One of the biggest challenges with AI governance is finding the balance between productivity and protection.

Organisations don’t necessarily want to block Copilot from searching the web.

The web is an important part of its usefulness.

Instead, the objective is to introduce a more intelligent control:

Allow users to benefit from AI while preventing sensitive information from being used in inappropriate external interactions.

That is a much more mature approach to AI governance than simply blocking AI services altogether.

Where Microsoft Purview fits

This is another example of why Microsoft Purview is becoming increasingly important in an organisation’s AI strategy.

Purview already provides organisations with capabilities around areas such as:

  • Data classification
  • Sensitivity labels
  • Data Loss Prevention
  • Information protection
  • Insider Risk Management
  • Compliance
  • Data lifecycle management

The new Copilot DLP capability extends that governance philosophy into an increasingly important AI scenario.

The fundamental principle remains the same:

Understand your data, classify it appropriately and apply controls based on its sensitivity.

Think about the scenario

Consider a user working with commercially sensitive information.

They ask Copilot something that requires external web information.

The question might contain information that, from a business perspective, should not be included in an external search.

With this new capability, Purview can act as a real-time control point.

Rather than relying entirely on the user to recognise the risk, the organisation can apply a policy-based control to prevent sensitive information from being used in that external web search.

That’s an important shift.

The control moves closer to the point where the risk occurs.

Another piece of the Copilot governance puzzle

This announcement shouldn’t be viewed in isolation.

Organisations building a Microsoft AI governance framework increasingly need to think about several layers:

1. Identity

Who is using Copilot?

2. Access

What information can that person access?

3. Data protection

How sensitive is that information?

4. AI interaction

What can Copilot do with that information?

5. External interaction

Can information be used in interactions with external services?

6. Monitoring

Can the organisation understand what is happening?

The new Purview DLP capability sits firmly within that data protection and AI interaction layer.

What should organisations be thinking about?

Although the roadmap announcement is primarily for awareness, it is worth considering whether your existing governance strategy is ready for this type of control.

Ask yourself:

Do we know what sensitive information exists across Microsoft 365?

Are our sensitivity labels being applied consistently?

Do our DLP policies adequately protect sensitive information?

Have we considered what happens when Copilot interacts with external web services?

Do our users understand the difference between asking Copilot about organisational information and asking it to use that information in an external interaction?

These questions become increasingly important as Copilot moves from an interesting productivity tool to a core part of everyday work.

The bigger picture

For me, the most interesting part of this announcement isn’t the individual DLP control.

It’s the direction Microsoft is taking.

We’re moving from:

“Should we allow AI?”

to:

“How do we allow AI safely?”

And increasingly:

“What should AI be allowed to do with each piece of information?”

That is where effective AI governance starts to become much more sophisticated.

The future isn’t necessarily about putting a wall around AI.

It’s about creating intelligent boundaries around data.

Microsoft Purview’s expanding integration with Copilot is a significant part of that journey.

Roadmap: RM565870
Capability: Microsoft Purview DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Chat

item.title: 🚨 Power Platform Cost Controls: Microsoft Introduces Tenant Credit Pool Governance
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft 365 Message Center ID: MC1458282General Availability: 26 August 2026 If your organisation is using Power Platform, Copilot Studio or AI-powered workloads, keeping control of capacity and consumption is becoming increasingly important. Microsoft is introducing a new Cost controls – Draw from tenant credit pool rule in the Power Platform admin center, giving administrators more […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft 365 Message Center ID: MC1458282
General Availability: 26 August 2026

If your organisation is using Power Platform, Copilot Studio or AI-powered workloads, keeping control of capacity and consumption is becoming increasingly important.

Microsoft is introducing a new Cost controls – Draw from tenant credit pool rule in the Power Platform admin center, giving administrators more control over how environments consume available tenant capacity.

And while Microsoft has classified this update as awareness only, it is worth understanding before it reaches general availability.

What is changing?

The new Draw from tenant credit pool capability allows administrators to decide whether an environment can use capacity from the organisation’s wider tenant credit pool when:

  • The environment reaches its allocated credit limit, or
  • The environment doesn’t have a specific credit allocation.

By default, the setting:

Draw from the available capacity in my tenant

will be enabled at the environment level.

This means an environment can potentially consume available capacity from the wider tenant pool once its own allocation has been exhausted.

Microsoft is now giving administrators the ability to change that behaviour.

Why does this matter?

This is fundamentally about cost and capacity governance.

As organisations increasingly deploy Copilot Studio agents, Power Platform automation and other AI capabilities, consumption can become harder to predict.

Without appropriate controls, an individual environment could potentially consume additional capacity from the tenant pool once its allocated credits have been used.

The new control gives organisations a choice:

Allow the environment to draw from the tenant pool

This provides greater flexibility and helps workloads continue operating when their allocated capacity is exhausted.

Prevent the environment from drawing from the tenant pool

This provides tighter cost control by limiting the credits that the environment can consume each month.

Neither option is universally “right”.

The important thing is that the decision becomes part of your Power Platform governance model.

Environment-level control

Administrators will be able to manage the capability for individual environments through the Power Platform admin center.

This provides a useful level of granularity where different environments have different requirements.

For example, you might decide:

Development environments

Don’t draw from the tenant pool.

Test environments

Don’t draw from the tenant pool unless specifically approved.

Critical production environments

Allow access to the tenant pool to reduce the risk of service disruption.

This is where the feature becomes particularly interesting from a governance perspective.

Rather than treating every environment identically, organisations can make decisions based on business criticality, consumption and risk.

But there is an important catch with Environment Groups

If you’re using Environment Groups, pay particular attention to this part.

When the rule is published for an Environment Group, the setting will apply across all environments within that group.

The individual environments will then no longer be able to change the setting themselves.

That means you need to think carefully about your group structure.

For example:

Production Environment Group
↓
Cost control rule enabled
↓
All environments inherit the setting

If you need individual environment-level control, Microsoft states that you should not apply the rule to that Environment Group, or alternatively move the environment outside the group.

This is more than a cost-control setting

For me, the interesting part of this announcement isn’t simply the new toggle.

It’s another example of Microsoft giving organisations increasingly granular controls over the AI and Power Platform estate.

As organisations move from experimenting with Copilot and agents to running them as production services, governance needs to evolve.

You need to start asking questions such as:

  • Which environments are allowed to consume tenant capacity?
  • Which environments should have hard consumption boundaries?
  • Who owns the consumption?
  • Which environments are business critical?
  • How much capacity should each environment receive?
  • What happens when an environment reaches its allocation?
  • Are Environment Groups being used appropriately?
  • Are we monitoring consumption closely enough to identify unexpected growth?

These are no longer simply Power Platform administration questions.

They’re becoming part of AI governance, financial governance and operational governance.

What should administrators do?

Microsoft says no action is required for this update.

However, I’d recommend using the announcement as an opportunity to review your current capacity governance.

1. Review your environments

Understand which environments are:

  • Development
  • Test
  • Production
  • Business critical
  • Experimental
  • No longer required

2. Review your Environment Groups

If you’re using Environment Groups, understand which environments inherit configuration from group-level rules.

3. Review your consumption model

Consider whether environments should be able to draw from the wider tenant pool when their allocation is exhausted.

4. Consider your governance policy

Don’t make the decision purely from a technical perspective.

Consider business criticality, cost, risk and user impact.

How do you configure it?

Microsoft states that administrators can configure the rule from:

Power Platform admin center → Manage → Environment Group

Select the relevant Environment Group and add:

Cost controls – Draw from tenant credit pool

You can then configure whether the setting is enabled or disabled and apply the changes.

Microsoft also states that Power Platform API methods can be used to manage the capability at scale.

The Jim Talks takeaway

The Power Platform is increasingly becoming an enterprise AI platform, not simply a collection of low-code tools.

As Copilot Studio agents and AI-powered workloads become embedded into everyday business processes, capacity management becomes governance.

The question is no longer simply:

“Can we build this agent?”

It’s increasingly:

“Can we govern what happens when thousands of people start using it?”

This new control is a small but important piece of that puzzle.


General Availability: 26 August 2026

Microsoft 365 Message Center: MC1458282

item.title: 🚨 Bringing Anthropic Claude Enterprise into Microsoft Purview: A Practical Deployment Guide
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: As organisations accelerate their adoption of generative AI, governance teams face a familiar challenge: how do you maintain visibility, compliance and security when business users are interacting with AI platforms outside of Microsoft 365? Microsoft Purview’s Anthropic Claude Enterprise connector helps address this challenge by bringing Claude activity and conversation data into the Microsoft Purview […]
item.content:encoded:
As organisations accelerate their adoption of generative AI, governance teams face a familiar challenge: how do you maintain visibility, compliance and security when business users are interacting with AI platforms outside of Microsoft 365?

Microsoft Purview’s Anthropic Claude Enterprise connector helps address this challenge by bringing Claude activity and conversation data into the Microsoft Purview ecosystem, enabling organisations to monitor usage, investigate activity, support compliance initiatives and strengthen AI governance.

In this article, we’ll explore the key considerations, prerequisites and validation steps required to successfully deploy the Anthropic Claude Enterprise connector in Microsoft Purview.

Why Connect Claude Enterprise to Microsoft Purview?

Many organisations are adopting multiple AI platforms to meet different business requirements. While this can increase productivity, it can also create governance blind spots.

The Anthropic Claude Enterprise connector enables Microsoft Purview to ingest data from Claude Enterprise, providing visibility into:

  • User activity and authentication events
  • Administrative actions
  • File uploads
  • AI interactions and conversation history
  • Compliance and audit-related information

This allows security, compliance and governance teams to extend oversight beyond the Microsoft ecosystem while maintaining a more unified view of AI usage across the organisation.

Start with Governance, Not Technology

Before deploying the connector, it is important to understand what data should be collected and why.

The connector supports two primary data scopes:

Activity Feed

The Activity Feed captures operational and audit information, including:

  • Authentication events
  • User interactions
  • Administrative actions
  • Compliance-related activity
  • File upload activity

This scope is particularly useful when organisations want to monitor adoption trends, user activity and overall platform usage.

Chat Conversations

Chat Conversations provide access to:

  • User prompts
  • Claude-generated responses
  • Conversation metadata
  • Message history

While this provides valuable insight into AI usage patterns, it also introduces additional privacy and governance considerations because conversation content may contain business-sensitive information.

A Critical Governance Decision

Before deployment, organisations should determine:

  • Whether both data scopes are required
  • Who will own the data
  • Who can access the imported information
  • How conversation data will be governed and reviewed
  • Whether the business has a clear justification for collecting conversation content

Many organisations find that conversation data represents the most sensitive aspect of an AI governance programme and should therefore be considered carefully before implementation.

Anthropic Prerequisites

Successful deployment begins within the Anthropic environment.

First, confirm that your organisation is using Claude Enterprise, as the connector does not support consumer or Team subscriptions.

You will also need to identify the Anthropic Primary Owner, who is responsible for configuring the Compliance API.

The primary configuration activities include:

  1. Enabling the Compliance API.
  2. Generating a Compliance Access Key.
  3. Identifying the correct Anthropic Organisation ID.

The Compliance Access Key should be treated as a privileged credential and handled using the same security standards applied to other integration secrets.

Avoid storing it in:

  • Documentation
  • Email messages
  • Teams conversations
  • Scripts
  • Screenshots

Microsoft Purview Requirements

On the Microsoft side, several prerequisites should be validated before connector deployment begins.

These include:

  • Appropriate Microsoft 365 and Purview licensing
  • Data Connector Admin permissions
  • Access to the Microsoft Purview portal
  • Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) permissions, where required
  • Microsoft Purview auditing enabled within the tenant

In addition, administrators should verify that the Anthropic Claude connector is available within the Data Connectors section of Microsoft Purview.

How Claude Data Supports Purview Capabilities

One common misconception is that the connector enables every Purview capability for Claude interactions.

In reality, the strongest value today lies in visibility, auditing and governance.

Supported areas include:

  • Data Security Posture Management (DSPM)
  • Auditing
  • Data Classification
  • Insider Risk Management
  • Communication Compliance
  • eDiscovery
  • Data Lifecycle Management
  • Compliance Manager

Organisations should view the integration primarily as a mechanism for monitoring, investigation and governance rather than a method for applying the full Microsoft Purview compliance stack directly to Claude interactions.

A Recommended Deployment Approach

Rather than configuring the connector immediately, organisations should follow a phased deployment model.

Phase 1: Anthropic Preparation

Confirm:

  • Claude Enterprise licensing
  • Primary Owner assignment
  • Compliance API activation
  • Compliance Access Key creation
  • Organisation ID identification
  • Agreed governance scope

Phase 2: Microsoft Preparation

Validate:

  • Licensing
  • Administrative permissions
  • Purview access
  • DSPM permissions
  • Auditing configuration

Phase 3: Connector Configuration

Within Microsoft Purview:

Settings → Data Connectors → All Connectors → Anthropic Claude → Add Connector

The configuration process requires:

  • Connector name
  • Compliance Access Key
  • Anthropic Organisation ID
  • API endpoint information
  • Data scope selection
  • Synchronisation frequency

A clear naming convention, such as “Anthropic Claude Enterprise – Production”, makes ongoing management significantly easier.

Phase 4: Validation

Deployment is not complete simply because the connector status shows as connected.

A structured validation exercise should confirm that:

  • Synchronisation is functioning correctly
  • Expected Claude activity is appearing
  • Activity Feed data is visible
  • Chat Conversation data is available where configured
  • DSPM reporting is being populated
  • Expected users and events can be located within Purview

Don’t Forget Post-Deployment Validation

One of the most common mistakes during connector deployments is assuming that a successful connection equals a successful implementation.

Instead, organisations should perform validation checks in both platforms.

Within Anthropic

Confirm:

  • Compliance API remains enabled
  • Access keys remain valid
  • Correct organisation configuration
  • Expected user activity exists

Within Microsoft Purview

Confirm:

  • Healthy connector status
  • Ongoing synchronisation
  • Activity Explorer visibility
  • DSPM data population
  • Expected user activity
  • Prompt and response visibility when conversation ingestion is enabled

It is also worth noting that data may not appear immediately. Microsoft guidance indicates that it can take approximately one day for information to begin populating DSPM reporting following connector configuration.

Security and Operational Best Practices

As with any governance integration, operational ownership is essential.

Organisations should:

  • Restrict connector administration to authorised personnel
  • Document approved data scopes
  • Review access permissions regularly
  • Assign clear ownership for monitoring and maintenance
  • Protect Compliance API credentials using secure credential management practices

Most importantly, stakeholders should understand exactly what information is being ingested, particularly where conversation content is included in scope.

The Jim Talks takeaway

As AI adoption continues to expand, visibility across multiple AI platforms will become an increasingly important governance requirement. The Anthropic Claude Enterprise connector for Microsoft Purview provides organisations with a practical way to extend their compliance, auditing and monitoring capabilities beyond Microsoft-native AI experiences.

By taking the time to address governance decisions, validate prerequisites and perform thorough post-deployment testing, organisations can establish a secure and well-governed foundation for managing Claude Enterprise activity within Microsoft Purview.

The result is greater transparency, stronger compliance oversight and increased confidence in how AI is being used across the business.

item.title: 📦 Azure Roadmap update: Azure PST Import Is Coming to Exchange Online – and It Changes How Administrators Handle Archived Email
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: If you’ve ever had to deal with PST files, you’ll know they have a habit of appearing at exactly the wrong time. Old Outlook archives. Historical mailboxes. Former employees. Data sitting on file shares or someone’s laptop. And eventually someone asks the inevitable question: “Can we get all of this email back into Microsoft 365?” […]
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever had to deal with PST files, you’ll know they have a habit of appearing at exactly the wrong time.

Old Outlook archives. Historical mailboxes. Former employees. Data sitting on file shares or someone’s laptop. And eventually someone asks the inevitable question:

“Can we get all of this email back into Microsoft 365?”

Microsoft is introducing Azure PST Import, providing administrators with a structured, PowerShell-based way to import PST files stored in Azure Blob Storage directly into Exchange Online mailboxes.

The new capability is designed to make the process more controlled and auditable, while adding an important step that administrators will appreciate:

You can analyse and validate the import before actually importing the data.

That’s a potentially significant improvement when you’re dealing with large quantities of historical email.

So, what is Azure PST Import?

At its simplest, Azure PST Import provides a way for administrators to take PST files stored in Azure Blob Storage and import their contents into Exchange Online mailboxes.

The process is administrator-driven and uses PowerShell cmdlets rather than a graphical user interface.

The basic workflow looks like this:

Azure Blob Storage → Analyse → Validate → Import → Report → Clean up

The idea is to provide administrators with greater confidence before the data actually lands in users’ mailboxes.

And when you’re dealing with historical email data, that’s a very useful capability.

Analyse first, import second

One of the more interesting aspects of the new experience is the Analyze mode.

Rather than immediately starting an import and discovering problems halfway through, administrators can first run a migration batch in Analyze mode.

This allows Microsoft 365 to validate the readiness of the import.

For example, the analysis can validate things such as:

  • Whether the specified PST files actually exist
  • PST file sizes
  • Whether the target mailbox is suitable
  • Whether the appropriate licence is assigned
  • Whether the mailbox is inactive or soft-deleted
  • Whether the recipient type is UserMailbox
  • Whether an archive is enabled when importing to an archive
  • Relevant mailbox quota requirements

That’s an important change in mindset.

Instead of:

“Let’s start the migration and see what happens.”

You can take the approach of:

“Let’s validate everything first.”

How does the process work?

The process is essentially broken into several stages.

1. Create the Azure PST Import endpoint

The first step is establishing the connection between Azure storage and Exchange Online.

Administrators create an Azure PST Import migration endpoint using PowerShell.

The endpoint setup also validates that the Azure storage account and container exist and are reachable.

There’s an important permission requirement here.

The Office 365 Import Service application needs the:

Storage Blob Data Reader

role on the target Azure storage account.

Without that permission, endpoint creation will fail.

So this is something worth checking before you start troubleshooting the migration itself.

2. Prepare your import files

You’ll need to prepare your batch input files, using XML and/or CSV, depending on the requirements of your import.

These files provide the information required to tell the service what should be imported and where it should go.

This is another area where preparation matters.

A little time spent getting your input files right can save considerably more time later.

3. Run the migration in Analyse mode

This is arguably the most useful part of the new workflow.

Rather than immediately importing the PST data, run the migration batch in:

Analyze

mode.

Microsoft can then validate the import and provide analysis results and reports.

This gives administrators the opportunity to identify potential problems before the actual import begins.

4. Review the results

Once analysis is complete, administrators can review the results and reports.

This is your opportunity to stop and fix anything that isn’t quite right.

Perhaps a mailbox doesn’t meet the requirements.

Perhaps a PST file isn’t where you expected it to be.

Perhaps a quota isn’t sufficient.

Perhaps the target mailbox isn’t in the correct state.

Whatever the issue, the idea is to discover it before starting the real import.

5. Create and start the import batch

Once you’re happy with the analysis results, you can use those results to create and start the actual import batch.

At that point, the PST files are imported into the specified Exchange Online mailboxes.

The process is controlled by administrators through PowerShell.

There is currently no graphical user interface for this experience.

And then comes the clean-up

Once the import has completed, administrators can perform the required post-import clean-up.

This is worth considering as part of the migration plan rather than treating it as an afterthought.

PST files have a habit of multiplying.

If you’ve ever discovered a folder containing:

Archive.pst
Archive-old.pst
Archive-final.pst
Archive-final-2.pst
Archive-final-REALLY-FINAL.pst

…you’ll understand why.

A structured import process gives organisations an opportunity to bring historical email into a more manageable Microsoft 365 environment.

What does this mean for compliance?

This is where Azure PST Import becomes particularly interesting from a Microsoft Purview and governance perspective.

Once PST content has been imported into Exchange Online, it becomes part of the mailbox environment.

That means the imported data is then subject to the existing behaviours and controls associated with the target mailbox.

According to Microsoft’s announcement, imported mailbox data becomes subject to existing:

  • Microsoft Purview retention policies
  • Retention labels
  • Holds
  • Deletion workflows

That could be particularly valuable for organisations that have historically had important business records sitting inside unmanaged PST files.

Instead of having historical information isolated inside individual PST files, the data can be brought into the Microsoft 365 environment where existing governance processes can apply.

What about auditing?

The change also provides administrators with existing audit and reporting capabilities.

Administrative activity relating to the PST import, along with resulting mailbox changes, can be monitored using existing:

Exchange Online audit logging

and

Microsoft Purview audit capabilities.

This is important from a compliance perspective because organisations don’t simply need to move data.

They may also need to demonstrate:

What was imported?

When was it imported?

Who performed the activity?

What happened to the data afterwards?

Being able to monitor the process using existing audit and reporting mechanisms helps support that requirement.

Who is this relevant to?

This update is particularly relevant to:

  • Microsoft 365 administrators
  • Exchange Online administrators
  • Organisations managing historical PST archives
  • Organisations importing PST data into user mailboxes
  • Organisations importing PST data into archive mailboxes
  • Teams responsible for Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management

There is no direct user action required.

This is an administrator-driven process.

There are some important prerequisites

Before jumping straight in, administrators should make sure the environment is ready.

You’ll need:

Azure storage

Your Azure storage account and container need to exist and be reachable.

Azure permissions

The Office 365 Import Service needs the Storage Blob Data Reader role on the target storage account.

Import files

Your XML and/or CSV batch input files need to be prepared correctly.

Mailbox readiness

The target mailbox needs to meet the required conditions.

That includes checking:

  • Appropriate licensing
  • Mailbox status
  • Recipient type
  • Archive status, where applicable
  • Archive quota
  • Recoverable Items quota

PST readiness

The PST files themselves also need to be checked.

Analysis validates that the specified PST files exist and validates their file size.

Why is this interesting from a governance perspective?

For me, the most interesting part of this isn’t actually the PST import itself.

It’s what happens after the PST is imported.

PST files have traditionally been a bit of an information governance headache.

They can contain years of email.

They can exist outside the normal Microsoft 365 governance framework.

They can be difficult to discover.

They can be difficult to manage consistently.

And they can sit quietly on a laptop or file share for years.

Moving that information into Exchange Online changes the conversation.

Once imported, the data becomes part of the Microsoft 365 environment and can fall under the organisation’s existing retention, hold, deletion and auditing processes.

In other words:

The goal isn’t just to move old email.

It’s to bring that information into a governed environment.

And that’s a much more interesting proposition.

What should administrators do now?

If your organisation has a significant PST estate, this is worth putting on the radar.

I’d start by asking a few simple questions:

How many PST files do we actually have?

Where are they?

Who owns them?

What information do they contain?

Do they contain records that need to be retained?

Are any subject to legal or regulatory requirements?

Which mailboxes should they ultimately belong to?

Do our current retention policies apply appropriately to the target mailboxes?

Those questions turn a technical migration into an information governance exercise.

And that’s exactly how I would approach it.

When is it coming?

Microsoft says the global rollout is expected to:

Begin: Late August 2026
Complete: Early September 2026

Microsoft 365 Roadmap ID: 565865

The experience is PowerShell-only and isn’t currently being delivered through a graphical administration interface.

The Jim Talks takeaway

PSTs aren’t going away overnight.

But perhaps we can finally start moving away from the idea of treating them as mysterious containers of historical email sitting somewhere on a network drive.

Azure PST Import gives administrators a structured path for bringing that information into Exchange Online.

And the really important part isn’t simply the ability to import it.

It’s the ability to analyse first, validate the destination, import in a controlled way, audit the activity and then bring that historical information under the organisation’s existing Microsoft 365 governance processes.

Because ultimately:

Moving information is migration.

Bringing it into a governed environment is information governance.

And that’s where this update gets interesting.

item.title: 🚨 Shadow AI: The AI Your Organisation Doesn’t Know It’s Using
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: “Are our employees using AI?” If your immediate answer is “Not really” or “We don’t think so”, you might want to keep reading. Because here’s the uncomfortable truth: AI adoption is moving much faster than most organisations can govern it. Employees are already using AI to write emails, summarise meetings, analyse spreadsheets, create presentations, write […]
item.content:encoded:
“Are our employees using AI?”

If your immediate answer is “Not really” or “We don’t think so”, you might want to keep reading.

Because here’s the uncomfortable truth:

AI adoption is moving much faster than most organisations can govern it.

Employees are already using AI to write emails, summarise meetings, analyse spreadsheets, create presentations, write code, research customers and generally make their working lives easier.

And why wouldn’t they?

If something takes an hour and AI can get it down to ten minutes, people are going to use it.

The problem isn’t necessarily that employees are doing something wrong.

The problem is that you might not know what they’re doing.

Welcome to the world of Shadow AI.

So… what exactly is Shadow AI?

Let’s keep this simple.

Shadow AI is AI being used without the knowledge, approval or governance of the organisation.

It could be an employee copying a customer email into a public AI chatbot and asking it to write a response.

It could be someone uploading a spreadsheet containing sensitive information and asking AI to analyse it.

It could be a developer using an AI coding assistant that hasn’t been approved.

Or someone in HR asking an online AI service to summarise a document containing employee information.

And here’s the interesting part:

They might not be trying to break any rules.

They might simply be trying to do their job.

They’ve found a tool that saves them time, makes their work easier or helps them solve a problem.

And that’s precisely why Shadow AI is such a difficult governance problem.

The employee isn’t necessarily the problem.

The lack of visibility is.

The uncomfortable truth

For years, we’ve built increasingly sophisticated controls around organisational information.

We ask:

Where is it stored?

Who can access it?

How is it protected?

How long should we keep it?

Then AI came along and changed the game.

Suddenly, an employee doesn’t necessarily need to give an AI system direct access to an information repository.

They can simply copy the information into the AI.

And that changes the governance question.

It is no longer just:

“Who has access to our information?”

It’s becoming:

“Where is our information going, what is being done with it, and who or what is processing it?”

That’s a much bigger question.

So what’s the actual risk?

There are three big ones.

1. Data leakage

This is the obvious one.

Someone takes sensitive information and puts it into an AI service outside the organisation’s controlled environment.

It might be:

  • Customer information
  • Financial data
  • Personal information
  • Intellectual property
  • Commercial plans
  • Internal documents
  • Source code

The employee might think:

“I’ll just paste this in and ask AI to summarise it.”

But suddenly the organisation has some serious questions to answer.

Where did the information go?

Who processed it?

What controls applied?

What happened to the output?

And perhaps most importantly:

Can we prove what happened?

2. Compliance gaps

Organisations have rules.

Regulatory requirements.

Contractual obligations.

Legal responsibilities.

Internal policies.

All of those things exist for a reason.

But here’s the problem:

Your policies don’t automatically follow your data into every AI tool on the internet.

If employees are using unmanaged AI services, there can be a significant gap between:

What your organisation says should happen

and

What is actually happening.

And that gap?

That’s where governance problems start.

3. You simply don’t know

This might actually be the biggest problem.

Which AI tools are people using?

Who is using them?

How often?

Why?

What information are they putting into them?

And are some employees regularly handling sensitive information through unmanaged AI?

If you don’t know the answers, you’re not really governing AI.

You’re guessing.

And guessing isn’t a particularly great governance strategy.

“But we have Microsoft 365 Copilot…”

Great.

That is an important part of your AI strategy.

But it doesn’t mean Shadow AI has disappeared.

Microsoft 365 Copilot is an enterprise AI capability designed to operate within the Microsoft 365 ecosystem and work with your organisation’s identity, permissions and security controls.

But here’s the important question:

What other AI are your employees using alongside Copilot?

Because an organisation can have a perfectly good Microsoft 365 Copilot deployment…

…and still have employees using external AI services every day.

That’s where the Shadow AI conversation gets interesting.

Here’s the Shadow AI paradox

People aren’t using Shadow AI because they hate their organisation.

They’re using it because it works.

Think about it.

You have a difficult email.

AI can help.

You’ve got a huge document.

AI can summarise it.

You’ve got a spreadsheet.

AI can analyse it.

You’ve got a presentation to create.

AI can help.

You’ve got some code that isn’t behaving.

AI might know why.

And if something takes an hour manually but five minutes with AI…

Which option do you think people are going to choose?

Exactly.

So here’s one of the most important things organisations need to understand:

You cannot govern AI effectively by pretending people won’t use it.

The technology is already here.

The challenge is creating an environment where people can use it safely and responsibly.

Should we just block everything?

Ah, the classic IT response. We’ve all been there right?

“Block it.”

Sometimes that’s absolutely the right answer.

But making “block AI” your entire strategy probably isn’t going to end well.

Because if employees are getting genuine value from AI, they’ll keep looking for ways to use it.

Block one application?

Another appears.

Don’t provide an approved alternative?

People find their own.

And suddenly you’ve pushed the behaviour further underground.

So perhaps the better question isn’t:

“How do we stop people using AI?”

It’s:

“How do we make it safe for people to use AI?”

That means providing trusted alternatives, protecting sensitive information, establishing clear guidance and applying sensible controls.

The first step isn’t blocking. It’s visibility.

Before you reach for the block button, ask a much more useful question:

“What AI are our employees actually using?”

That’s where things get interesting.

You want to understand:

Which tools are being used?

Who is using them?

How often?

Why?

What information could be involved?

Which applications represent the greatest risk?

Once you have those answers, Shadow AI stops being an abstract concern.

It becomes something you can actually measure, understand and manage.

From “we think” to “we know”

Imagine asking your organisation:

“Are employees using AI tools outside Microsoft 365?”

Someone might respond:

“Probably not very much.”

Hmm.

Now imagine being able to say:

“We’ve identified 1,200 employees interacting with external AI applications over the last 90 days.”

Different conversation, isn’t it?

Now you can ask:

Which applications?

Which departments?

Which users?

Which applications are approved?

Which aren’t?

Where is sensitive information involved?

Where do we need controls?

This is why discovery is the turning point.

It takes you from:

Assumption → Evidence

And that’s where real governance begins.

Control the apps. Control the data.

Once you understand what’s happening, you’ve got something much more useful than a list of scary headlines.

You’ve got information you can act on.

I think about Shadow AI governance around two fundamental questions.

1. Which AI applications are we comfortable with?

Assess them against things like:

  • Security
  • Privacy
  • Data handling
  • Compliance
  • Vendor risk
  • Business need
  • Regulatory requirements
  • Organisational policy

Then classify them.

Approved.

Restricted.

Monitored.

Blocked.

Because not every AI application presents the same risk.

2. What information can people put into them?

This might actually be the more important question.

Imagine two prompts.

“Rewrite this generic paragraph.”

Pretty harmless.

Now:

“Summarise this document containing confidential customer information.”

Same AI tool.

Very different risk.

That’s why AI governance and information governance are so closely connected.

Classification.

Sensitivity labels.

DLP.

Access controls.

Retention.

Monitoring.

Audit.

All suddenly become part of the AI conversation.

The question changes from:

“Can I use this AI tool?”

to:

“What am I allowed to put into this AI tool?”

And that is a much more mature governance conversation.

The biggest Shadow AI mistake

It’s tempting to think the answer is simply:

Block.

But blocking everything isn’t governance.

It’s a reaction.

A better model is:

Discover → Assess → Govern → Protect → Monitor

First, understand what is happening.

Then assess the risk.

Decide what controls are appropriate.

Protect the information that matters.

And keep monitoring.

Because AI isn’t standing still.

New applications will appear.

Existing applications will gain new capabilities.

Employees will discover new ways of using them.

And increasingly, AI agents will be able to interact with business systems and information.

The Shadow AI challenge isn’t going away.

It’s probably going to get more interesting.

This isn’t just an IT problem

Here’s another thing worth remembering.

Shadow AI touches almost everyone.

IT

Which applications are being used?

Security

What risks do they introduce?

Information Governance

What information is being processed?

Compliance

Are our obligations being met?

HR

What are employees permitted to do?

Legal

What are our obligations around data and intellectual property?

Business Leadership

How do we capture the productivity benefits without taking unnecessary risks?

This isn’t something you can simply throw over the wall to the IT department.

AI governance needs a joined-up approach.

And then there’s Copilot…

This is where things get particularly interesting for Microsoft 365 organisations.

Microsoft 365 Copilot provides an enterprise AI capability within the Microsoft ecosystem.

But there’s an important point:

Copilot can work with the information the user already has access to.

So if your Microsoft 365 environment contains years of overshared documents, messy permissions and information that has accumulated without proper governance…

Copilot doesn’t magically clean that up.

In fact, AI could make those existing issues far more visible and potentially more consequential.

Which brings us to a rather important question:

Are you ready for AI to help people discover the information they already have access to?

Where does Purview fit?

This is where Microsoft Purview becomes particularly interesting.

Purview can form an important part of the wider information governance strategy, helping organisations understand, protect and govern their information.

But I wouldn’t think of Purview simply as another security product.

Think of it as part of your organisation’s information control layer.

Ask:

Where is our sensitive information?

How is it classified?

Who can access it?

How is it being shared?

What policies apply?

What needs to be retained?

What needs to be deleted?

What happens when we need to investigate something?

And increasingly:

“How should this information be governed when AI gets involved?”

Because AI governance without information governance is going to be difficult.

You can’t safely govern AI if you don’t understand the information AI is interacting with.

So what should organisations actually do?

Don’t panic.

You don’t need to solve every AI governance problem tomorrow.

Start somewhere sensible.

01 – Get visibility

Find out which AI applications are being used.

Don’t guess.

Find the evidence.

02 – Find your highest-risk scenarios

Focus on sensitive information, regulated data and intellectual property.

03 – Give people safe alternatives

If employees are using AI because it makes them more productive, give them an approved way to achieve the same outcome.

04 – Protect the data

Use the controls already available to you – information protection, DLP, classification and appropriate access controls.

05 – Give people clear guidance

Don’t just tell employees:

“You can’t do this.”

Tell them:

“Here’s what you can do.”

06 – Keep watching

AI governance isn’t a project with a completion date.

The landscape will keep moving.

The goal isn’t to stop AI

This is probably the biggest message I’d take away from the whole Shadow AI conversation.

The goal isn’t to stop employees using AI.

It isn’t to block every application.

And it certainly isn’t to write a 50-page AI policy that nobody reads.

The goal is much simpler:

Make AI useful, safe and governable.

Understand what’s happening.

Protect the information that matters.

Provide trusted alternatives.

And put sensible controls around the technology.

That’s the sweet spot.

And then things get really interesting…

We’re still relatively early in the AI journey.

Today’s Shadow AI might be an employee copying text into a chatbot.

Tomorrow?

It could be an AI agent connecting to multiple business systems, accessing information, making decisions and taking actions on someone’s behalf.

Suddenly, the questions become very different.

Not just:

“What information did the employee give the AI?”

But:

“What information can the agent access?”

“What can it do?”

“Who authorised it?”

“What decisions did it make?”

“What actions did it take?”

And perhaps the most important question of all:

“Can we prove what happened?”

You can’t govern what you can’t see

And perhaps that’s what Shadow AI really comes down to.

It isn’t fundamentally an AI problem.

It’s a visibility, information and governance problem that AI has brought into the spotlight.

The organisations that get this right won’t necessarily be the ones with the biggest list of blocked applications.

They’ll be the ones that understand:

What AI is being used.

Who is using it.

Why they’re using it.

What information is involved.

What risks exist.

And what controls are appropriate.

Because let’s face it…

Your employees are probably already using AI.

The real question is:

Do you know how?

And are you ready to govern what happens next?

You can’t govern what you can’t see.

And as AI becomes an increasingly important part of everyday work, seeing, understanding and governing AI activity could become one of the defining challenges of modern Microsoft 365 governance.

The Jim Talks takeaway

Don’t start your AI governance journey by asking, “What should we block?”

Start by asking, “What is actually happening?”

Visibility first. Governance second. Control follows.

item.title: Taking inspiration from… Saw 5?
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Yes, you read that right. Again, hear me out. I am a big believer in shared interests and finding things we can enjoy with others. When the chance came to watch a horror film with a loved one, I was sure it was something we could enjoy and discuss afterwards. The film came and went. […]
item.content:encoded:
Yes, you read that right. Again, hear me out.

I am a big believer in shared interests and finding things we can enjoy with others. When the chance came to watch a horror film with a loved one, I was sure it was something we could enjoy and discuss afterwards.

The film came and went. However, something quite unexpected happened… I was inspired, and not in a “movie” type of way.

The film follows a group of people trapped in a situation where they must overcome challenges to survive. Then came an incredible revelation: the challenges were never designed for individuals to overcome alone. They were designed for the group to work together, allowing everyone to make it to the end.

Whilst taking some time to reflect on that, I found myself applying that principle to daily life. We all face problems every day, and we all could benefit from each other’s experiences.

The problems I am experiencing today are the problems someone experienced yesterday, and someone else will experience tomorrow.

That is how we can look after each other. Knowledge sharing, reassurance, simply leaning on each other.  

None of us have to solve everything alone. Sometimes the answer we need is sitting with someone who has already faced the same challenge…

And that is the value of helping others: we don’t just solve problems for people; we make sure fewer people have to face them alone.

People are better when we stop seeing each other as obstacles and start seeing each other as support.

Who’d have thought that Saw 5 of all things would have given such a powerful message?

item.title: 🔍 Troubleshooting Microsoft Purview eDiscovery Just Got Easier
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: If you’ve ever spent far too long trying to work out why an eDiscovery case isn’t behaving as expected, a new Microsoft Purview update could make life considerably easier. Microsoft is introducing self-service diagnostics for eDiscovery, designed to help administrators identify and resolve some of the common configuration issues that can prevent eDiscovery from working […]
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever spent far too long trying to work out why an eDiscovery case isn’t behaving as expected, a new Microsoft Purview update could make life considerably easier.

Microsoft is introducing self-service diagnostics for eDiscovery, designed to help administrators identify and resolve some of the common configuration issues that can prevent eDiscovery from working as expected.

So, what’s changing?

The new diagnostic experience will help administrators troubleshoot areas including:

  • Case permissions – identify potential permission-related issues.
  • Security filters – highlight configuration problems that could affect search and discovery.
  • Policy status and configuration – identify potential issues with relevant policies and their configuration.

Rather than having to manually work through multiple settings and configurations, the new experience will highlight potential problems and provide guided recommendations to help resolve them.

Why does this matter?

As I am sure many of us know, eDiscovery can become complicated very quickly.

When a search doesn’t return the expected results, or a user can’t access the information they need, the underlying cause isn’t always immediately obvious. Is it a permissions issue? A security filter? A policy that hasn’t been configured correctly?

Previously, troubleshooting could involve working through multiple areas of the Microsoft Purview environment before finding the problem.

The introduction of self-service diagnostics brings some of that troubleshooting directly into the product.

That means administrators should be able to identify common issues faster, understand what’s causing them and take appropriate corrective action without immediately resorting to lengthy investigations or support cases.

Another step towards a more manageable Purview experience

This is perhaps not the most headline-grabbing Microsoft 365 update, but for the people who actually administer eDiscovery, it’s the type of improvement that can make a significant difference.

Microsoft Purview continues to become increasingly capable — but as functionality grows, configuration and troubleshooting can become increasingly complex.

Anything that helps administrators understand “why isn’t this working?” more quickly is therefore a welcome addition.

And there’s an interesting broader trend here: Microsoft is increasingly building guided diagnostics and recommendations directly into its compliance and governance tooling, helping administrators move from simply identifying problems to understanding how to resolve them.

When is it coming?

Public Preview: October 2026
General Availability: November 2026
Microsoft 365 Roadmap: 565222

The takeaway

eDiscovery is powerful — but power brings complexity.

Self-service diagnostics won’t remove that complexity, but it should make some of the most common troubleshooting scenarios considerably easier to navigate.

For organisations relying heavily on Microsoft Purview for compliance, investigations and eDiscovery, this is a small but useful improvement worth keeping an eye on.
